title: AWS Cannot Restore Data Held Only in Damaged Middle East Availability Zones
gist: Amazon Web Services has told customers that data held exclusively in war-damaged availability zones of its UAE (me-central-1) and Bahrain (me-south-1) regions is permanently unrecoverable, because the damage exceeded what its regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand. The episode turns multi-AZ redundancy marketing into a concrete liability question and exposes a hard conflict between data-residency law and cross-region backup.

insights.claim: Amazon Web Services has declared data hosted exclusively in the mec1-az2 availability zone of its UAE me-central-1 region permanently unrecoverable, while still working to recover regional resources and the other two zones mec1-az1 and mec1-az3.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: First public case of an AWS zone declaring customer data gone for good - a precedent for cloud liability, insurance and enterprise DR budgets.
insights.quote: After a thorough assessment, we have determined that we are unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted exclusively in the mec1-az2 availability zone.
insights.locator: For the UAE region, AWS wrote

insights.claim: In Bahrain the loss covers the entire me-south-1 region rather than a single zone, because the physical damage spanned multiple availability zones at once.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Region-level total loss invalidates the standard enterprise assumption that a region is the unit of durability.
insights.quote: The damage to our infrastructure spanned multiple availability zones and exceeded what our regional and multi-AZ services are designed to withstand.
insights.locator: For Bahrain, the assessment covers the whole region

insights.claim: Iranian drone strikes reported in March damaged three AWS data centres across the UAE and Bahrain regions, with two of three UAE availability zones significantly impaired, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed a second attack on the Bahrain region in July.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Repeat targeting means the exposure is ongoing, not a one-off - price Gulf-region cloud capacity and its insurance accordingly.
insights.locator: InfoQ reported in March that Iranian drone strikes

insights.claim: AWS is replacing the affected infrastructure and says service restoration updates will come over the coming months, with further detail on Bahrain only in early 2027, implying a multi-quarter capacity hole in regions opened in 2019 (Bahrain) and 2022 (UAE).
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Customers needing Gulf capacity have no credible AWS restoration date, which opens a window for regional and sovereign cloud competitors.
insights.locator: AWS says it is replacing the affected infrastructure

insights.claim: A resurfaced 2025 television interview shows an AWS leader telling viewers customers would not notice if an unmarked AWS data centre were destroyed, a claim now directly contradicted by unrecoverable customer data.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Public gap between vendor assurance and outcome is the kind of evidence that drives contract renegotiation and regulatory attention.
insights.quote: Yeah, you wouldn't notice. I mean, we might be a bit upset, but you wouldn't notice!
insights.locator: A 2025 television interview with an AWS leader

insights.claim: The prevailing misconception among engineering teams is that using AWS is itself a redundancy strategy, when the provider supplies components that customers must assemble into catastrophe resilience themselves.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of DR reassessments and spend on multi-region tooling, backup and resilience vendors.
insights.quote: They don't realize that AWS is a toolbox, not a 'ready made solution for redundancy against all catastrophes you are possibly exposed to'.

insights.claim: S3 Standard and related storage classes replicate objects across a minimum of three availability zones with a stated durability of 99.999999999% per year, but both the replication and the durability figure are regional properties that say nothing about surviving loss of the region.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The famous eleven-nines number is scoped, not absolute - a useful lens when auditing any vendor durability SLA.

insights.claim: Cloud providers are blamed for creating the executive-level impression of automatic resilience through marketing and conference channels, in the same way AI narratives have reached executives over the past two years.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A reminder that vendor narrative, not documentation, sets buyer expectations - and that the correction cycle can be abrupt.
insights.quote: Who is a CEO going to believe? Amazon, Microsoft and the entire IT infra division or that lone SRE who disagrees with them?

insights.claim: Outsourcing storage hands the performance-versus-correctness trade-off to a provider who is weighted toward the properties customers actually perceive, so invisible durability measures lose to visible latency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Structural reason to expect under-provisioned deep redundancy across all hyperscalers, not just AWS.
insights.quote: You won't notice that theres a third commit server off-site (unless that site is bombed), but you will notice slower writes.
insights.locator: Commenter dijit offered a structural explanation

insights.claim: The exposure demonstrated in the Middle East is geographic rather than contractual, so switching hyperscalers does not mitigate it: whoever could destroy ME-CENTRAL could as easily destroy an Azure or any other data centre in the same geography.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Multi-cloud within one conflict-exposed geography is not diversification; only distance is.
insights.quote: The risk is regional, not tied to a provider. The folks who took out ME-CENTRAL can just as easily take out Azure or any other data center.
insights.locator: Gregor Hohpe, co-author of Enterprise Integration Patterns

insights.claim: Multi-AZ architecture spreads a workload across facilities within roughly 100 kilometres of each other, which covers power outages, lightning strikes, tornadoes and earthquakes but not an attacker able to reach several of those facilities in one night.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The 100km radius is the concrete test for whether a resilience design covers kinetic or geopolitical threat models.
insights.locator: Six months on, that framing has a concrete outcome

themes.theme: Data residency as a hard constraint

insights.claim: Customers bound by data-residency rules that require information to stay within national borders could not have replicated out of the damaged regions at all, and encrypted offshore backups do not solve it because the decryption keys would also have to sit outside the jurisdiction to be usable after a regional loss.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sovereignty regulation creates an uninsurable residual risk class - watch for demand for in-country second sites and sovereign cloud build-outs.

insights.claim: Moving workloads out of a region during a crisis can restore service while pushing sensitive data outside national borders, and data residency is law rather than best practice, so the crisis response can itself be the compliance breach.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: DR runbooks in regulated industries need a legal sign-off path, not just a technical one.
insights.locator: A senior cloud architect at T-Systems International

insights.claim: The practical audit test is narrower than a multi-region strategy: identify anything that currently sits in one region with no copy elsewhere, then ask whether regulation or contract permits a copy to leave the jurisdiction; where it does not, the exposure belongs in a risk register rather than a runbook.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A concrete two-question due-diligence checklist for assessing any cloud-dependent business's catastrophic data risk.
